CONTROL SYSTEMS / VEHICLE DYNAMICS

Lateral Vehicle Control
with Model Predictive Control

Six steering controllers. Four driving scenarios. Six robustness cases. An interactive, reproducible comparison on a nonlinear vehicle model.

MATLABNonlinear MPCVehicle Dynamics144 Runs

Six steering controllers, four roads, six kinds of trouble

Project notes, October 2026

This is the second version of my lateral-control project. The first was a single MPC block in Simulink. This one compares six controllers, from pure pursuit to a real-time nonlinear MPC, on a nonlinear vehicle model with saturating tyres and a rate-limited steering actuator. Each controller drives four scenarios under six robustness cases: 144 runs in total.

Controllerspure pursuit, Stanley, LQR (gain-scheduled), linear MPC (fixed 15 m/s model), adaptive MPC (time-varying model), nonlinear MPC (real-time iteration)
Vehicle1600 kg single-track model, Fiala tyres, 50 ms steering lag, 0.8 rad/s rate limit, ±0.5 rad steering
Control rate20 Hz (plant integrated at 500 Hz)
MPC2 s horizon (40 steps), 10 free moves, curvature preview, lane corridor around obstacles as a soft constraint

1. The controllers

Six controllers, in increasing order of how much of the vehicle they model:

  • Pure pursuit picks a look-ahead point on the path and steers the front wheel at it geometrically. No model of the vehicle, no notion of speed or tyre grip.
  • Stanley adds a term for heading error on top of lateral error, both measured at the front axle. Still geometric, still no dynamics.
  • LQR (gain-scheduled) linearises the lateral-dynamics error model around the current speed and solves for a fixed optimal feedback gain. It reacts to the current error but does not look ahead or enforce limits.
  • Linear MPC predicts the error dynamics forward over a 2 s horizon using a single linear model fixed at 15 m/s, and solves a constrained QP every step. The fixed-speed linearisation is its main weakness, visible on the wet hairpin below.
  • Adaptive MPC is the same linear MPC, but the model is relinearised every step around the current speed instead of a fixed 15 m/s.
  • Nonlinear MPC predicts with the full nonlinear single-track model, including the Fiala tyre model losing grip, solved as a real-time-iteration nonlinear program.

Modelling more of the vehicle costs more compute per control step. The real-time budget here is 50 ms (20 Hz control rate); every controller has to fit inside that on one core of the reference Python implementation.

Lateral error against distance travelled, nominal case, all six controllers, on each of the four scenarios. This is the real per-run output, not a conceptual sketch: pure pursuit and Stanley oscillate because they only track the centreline; the MPCs stay tight on the open road and deliberately swing wide around the parked cars, which is exactly the corridor-constraint behaviour described in section 3.

The same comparison as actual driven paths, one controller at a time, picked to show the clearest contrast per scenario.

3. Ablation

Each controller ran every scenario under six conditions: nominal, sensor noise, model mismatch, 100 ms actuation delay (compensated and not), and all three combined. The full breakdown by scenario and condition is the heatmap grid in the next section; the case that separates the controllers most is delay, so it's shown here as actual trajectories rather than just an RMS number.

4. Benchmark

RMS lateral error for every controller and case on the three path-tracking scenarios. Cells marked “off” are runs where the car left the road (more than 6 m off the centreline).

5. What I learned

Delay matters more than anything else for the model-based controllers

A 100 ms steering delay with no compensation makes LQR and both linear MPCs leave the road in the 20 m/s lane change, and makes the nonlinear MPC’s error about 20 times larger. Predicting the state forward over the commands still in the delay (a few lines of code) brings all of them back to roughly their nominal accuracy. Pure pursuit and Stanley use the same command either way, and their low gains make them barely sensitive to the delay.

Modelling the tyres pays off near the limit

On the S-curves and under combined disturbances, the nonlinear MPC has the lowest error, because its prediction includes the tyres losing grip. On the wet hairpin, the fixed-speed linear MPC is the weakest MPC (0.19 m against 0.05 m), since the speed there ranges from 7 to 17 m/s while its model assumes 15. Scheduling the model on the upcoming speed, as the adaptive MPC does, removes most of that gap at no extra cost.

Only the MPCs can use the space around the path

Pure pursuit, Stanley and LQR only follow the centreline, so they drive through the parked cars. The MPCs treat the lane as a corridor that narrows next to each obstacle, and pass with 0.57–1.0 m of clearance in every case. That comparison isn’t entirely fair: with a planner giving them an avoidance path, the classic controllers would avoid the cars too. It does show what constraints in the optimizer buy you.

All of it runs in real time

Even the nonlinear MPC, the most expensive controller here, runs in about 14 ms against the 50 ms budget (Figure 1, section 1). There's headroom to spare on a single core of a reference Python implementation, let alone a compiled one.

6. Running it

The project is plain MATLAB with no toolboxes; the QP solver and LQR are included. From the repository folder:

setup_paths
run main/main_demo.m                                  % all controllers on the wet hairpin

res = run_scenario(default_config(), 'obstacles', 'nmpc');
plot_run(res); animate_run(res)

T = run_benchmark();                                  % all 144 runs, CSVs and figures in results/

The numbers on this page come from the Python reference implementation in tools/python_reference/, which mirrors the MATLAB code with the same models, gains and scenarios.

Vehicle: single-track model with Fiala tyres, no load transfer or combined slip. Lateral error is measured from the centreline, so on the obstacle scenario it includes the deliberate swerves. Noise cases use one random seed.
